title: GC modes in microservices
hook: You do not tune the GC by calling Collect in a controller. You pick a flavor (workstation vs server), a latency-versus-throughput stance, and container heap limits — then you measure.

sections.heading: What you can actually change
sections.prose: Server GC (DOTNET_gcServer=1, the ASP.NET Core default) creates per-processor heaps and is the right starting point for Kestrel APIs. Workstation GC (gcServer=0) uses less memory and is reasonable for tiny workers or client tools. Background GC is on by default for both in modern .NET and lets gen-2 work overlap mutators more than the old blocking mode. SustainedLowLatency and LowLatency trade pause behavior against heap growth; they are process-wide and easy to misuse. .NET 9 and 10 ship DATAS (dynamic adaptation to application sizes) so server GC can shrink heaps when traffic is quiet — useful when a service scales from 199 to 999 users and back. GCHeapHardLimit and GCHeapHardLimitPercent, plus container memory limits, stop the process from believing it has the whole VM. COMPlus_/DOTNET_ runtime knobs belong in the container spec, not in request code.

snippets.label: Observe, do not Collect
snippets.explanation: Logging IsServerGC and LatencyMode in diagnostics is fair. GC.Collect(2, GCCollectionMode.Forced, true) on each SQS message is not.

sections.heading: What you should not change
sections.prose: Do not force full collections after every Redis miss. Do not switch LatencyMode to LowLatency for the duration of a request and forget to restore it. Do not assume Workstation GC ‘has shorter pauses’ under 999 concurrent users — you may simply allocate from one heap and stall. Pin CPU count in Kubernetes so server GC heap count matches the cgroup, or you over-create heaps. Native AOT still uses the same GC family; it does not remove gen 2. When RSS grows, profile allocations and static roots first; GC mode is the second conversation.

interviewTakeaways: Server GC for multi-core services; workstation for small clients; confirm with GCSettings.IsServerGC.
Set heap hard limits in containers; pair with cgroup memory.
DATAS and latency modes are process settings. Collect in production request paths is a red flag.
commonPitfalls: Leaving Server GC on a 256 MB sidecar so heaps never shrink (mitigate with DATAS and hard limits).
Copying old gcConcurrent config folklore without checking current runtime defaults.
Matching ‘we called GC.Collect after SkiaSharp’ instead of Dispose.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node exposes flags like --max-old-space-size. There is no workstation versus server GC toggle analogous to DOTNET_gcServer. You still set a heap cap in containers.
